messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It happened on a Tuesday evening in late October. Drew had just finished a parent-teacher conference at the suburban elementary school where he worked as a special education teacher, and he was walking the three blocks to his car in the faculty parking lot. A man came out of the alley between two houses, shoving Drew against the brick wall of a garage. The impact sent a jolt through his neck, a sharp crack that he would feel for weeks afterward. The man was shouting—not words that Drew could parse later, just a furious, chaotic noise close to his face—while he ripped Drew’s messenger bag off his shoulder and punched him twice in the side of the head. Then he was gone, and Drew was on his knees on the cold pavement, his neck burning, his ears ringing, and the world feeling suddenly, impossibly wrong.

In the months that followed, that moment became a kind of fixed point that Drew could not stop returning to. The memory was not fuzzy or fragmented; it arrived in his mind like a series of clear, almost surgical photographs—the exact pattern of the brick, the angle of the streetlight, the man’s jacket riding up as he grabbed the bag. Drew could see it all in perfect stillness, but the stillness itself was horrifying, because it meant he was trapped inside the image, watching himself fail to do anything. He would feel a rising, helpless rage when the memory surfaced, a heat that made his hands tremble, but the rage always curdled quickly into a cold guilt. He should have seen it coming. He should have taken a different route. A smarter person, a stronger person, would not have been vulnerable in the first place. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. The thought drilled into him, and he began to believe it was true.

The consequences showed up first in small things. He stopped walking to his car after dark, asking a colleague to walk with him, and then stopped staying late at school altogether. The shouting of children in his classroom—something that had never bothered him before—began to make his heart race. During a meltdown from a nonverbal student, a high-pitched shriek sent him into a cold sweat, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stood gripping the sink, seeing those brick patterns behind his eyes. He started scanning every room he entered for exits, not consciously at first, but soon he could not stop. The faculty lounge, the grocery store, his own apartment—he would note the doors, the windows, the hallway to the fire escape, a low-level calculation running constantly in the back of his mind. His neck, which had healed physically, remained a source of somatic tension; whenever he felt a twinge, he would be pulled back into that alley, and he would have to talk himself down from a full flashback.

The hypervigilance became a way of life. Drew could not relax, even at home with the door locked and the chain on. He kept the television on for noise, but he still found himself sitting rigid on the couch, listening for footsteps, for a raised voice outside. He had come to believe that he could never let his guard down again, because his guard was the only thing that had failed. The word *inadequate* had lodged itself in his mind. He was a special education teacher, someone trained to stay calm under pressure, to anticipate chaos and manage it—and yet he had frozen, had been helpless. The shame of it coiled inside him.

At work, his colleagues noticed the change. He stopped volunteering for after-school duties. He became short with a paraprofessional who once joked about the school’s security cameras. He avoided the hallway near the main office where the school resource officer stood, because the sight of a police uniform sent a bolt of alert through him—not relief, but a kind of dread, as though the police themselves were part of the threat landscape. He knew this was irrational, but the feeling was too strong to argue with. The biggest consequence came when he failed to attend a mandatory staff training on crisis intervention; he told his supervisor he had a migraine, but the truth was he had seen the training involved role-playing a physical restraint, and the thought of someone shouting in his face made him nauseous. His supervisor was sympathetic, but it was a formal warning.

Drew is seeking help now because he is tired. He is tired of the constant scanning, of the guilt that follows every memory, of the way his life has shrunk to a narrow corridor of safe routines. He came to the clinic three weeks after a flashback in a grocery store—a teenager shouted to a friend across the aisle, and Drew dropped his cart and stood frozen, seeing the alley, feeling the brick against his back. He sat in the intake room with his hands clasped, his eyes moving to the door every few seconds, and said he wanted to stop being afraid of his own mind. What he fears most, he admitted, is that the guilt is right—that he is inadequate, that someone else would have handled it, that the mugging revealed something true about him. What he hopes for is to prove that wrong, to walk into a room and not count the exits, to hear a shout and not fall backward into that October night.
